needs.title: Washrooms that cope with the whole team
needs.body: An office washroom takes far more use than a home bathroom, and most of it comes in a few busy periods. Cisterns and flush valves wear, push taps stick, and urinal cisterns can run all night if nothing controls them. The Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 expect suitable toilets and washing facilities with hot and cold, or warm, water for staff. When one cubicle is out of use, the queue for the rest grows fast.

needs.title: Kitchenettes and drinks points
needs.body: Most offices run on one small kitchen: a sink, a dishwasher, perhaps a boiling water tap or a plumbed-in coffee machine and a fridge with a water feed. Each appliance needs a proper isolation valve, a sound waste connection and, where the supply feeds a machine, the right backflow protection. Hard London water scales up boiling water taps and dishwasher elements, so a filter or softener on the feed often means fewer breakdowns.

needs.title: Hot water where people wash their hands
needs.body: Many offices heat water with a small unvented cylinder or with under-sink point-of-use heaters at each basin. Point-of-use heaters are handy but can fail quietly, leaving one basin cold for weeks before anyone reports it. A single cylinder serving several floors can mean long pipe runs and a wait for warm water. We look at how your water is heated, how far it travels and whether a new heater would need its own circuit.

needs.title: Comfortable temperatures all year
needs.body: South-facing glass, a comms cupboard and a room full of laptops can make an office stuffy by lunchtime, while an ageing boiler may struggle on winter mornings. Our Gas Safe engineers work on domestic-sized boilers and heating, which covers many small offices. Larger commercial boiler plant needs engineers with commercial gas qualifications, and we will tell you straight if yours is beyond what we do. Our F-Gas certified engineers fit and maintain split air conditioning.

guidance.title: Planning a washroom refurbishment
guidance.body: If your washroom looks tired or keeps breaking down, a refurbishment is usually easier to manage than a string of emergency calls. Think about how many people use it at peak times, whether you need an accessible WC, and where the extractor fan will vent. Concealed cisterns behind panels look neat but need access hatches for later repairs. We can refit in stages, so one washroom stays open while another is worked on, and do the noisy work out of hours.

guidance.title: Who is responsible in a rented office
guidance.body: In a multi-let building, the landlord or managing agent often looks after the rising main, the drains and any shared heating, while tenants handle fittings inside their own space. Your lease sets out who does what, so check it before booking work on shared pipes. If water comes through your ceiling from the floor above, turn off your own supply if it helps, move equipment clear and tell the building manager. We can trace the source for whichever party is responsible.

guidance.title: Small checks that prevent bigger problems
guidance.body: Once a month, ask someone to look under the kitchenette sink and behind the dishwasher for drips or swollen boards. Listen for a toilet or urinal that keeps refilling, which wastes water. Cyclists' showers that are rarely used should be run for a few minutes each week, because stagnant water raises legionella risk, and the employer or landlord has a duty to manage that risk under HSE guidance. We can remove dead legs and fit thermostatic mixing valves where needed.

If you have a basement with a sump pump, test it by pouring water into the sump and watching it start. Clean air conditioning filters as the manufacturer advises, and book a service each year.

We fit dedicated hand-wash basins with lever or sensor taps close to prep areas, add a small water heater where hot water does not reach, and route the waste so it drains freely.

needs.title: Dishwashers, glasswashers and coffee machines
needs.body: Commercial dishwashers and glasswashers need a steady water feed, a waste that copes with a fast discharge and, in London's hard water, softening to stop scale building up on elements and spray arms. Espresso machines need a mains cold feed, an isolating valve, a filter cartridge and a drain point. The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 require backflow protection matched to the fluid risk, so each connection needs to be right, not just a quick tee.

needs.title: Hot water that keeps up with service
needs.body: A café can use most of its hot water in a short rush: washing up, hand washing and cleaning down all at once. An old cylinder with slow recovery, or one small instantaneous heater, runs cold just when you need it most. We look at your peak demand, your space and your electrical supply before suggesting a larger cylinder, extra point-of-use heaters or a mix of both. New heaters often need a dedicated circuit, which our electricians install.

needs.title: Backwash units that work every wash
needs.body: Most salon plumbing calls start at the backwash. Tilting basins crack at the pivot, mixer cartridges wear out from constant use, spray hoses split and the flexible connections behind the unit weep into the floor. When you refit or add a station, each unit needs isolating valves you can reach, a waste with enough fall, and a spray handset with backflow protection so dirty water can't be drawn back into the supply. needs.title: Waste pipes that cope with hair
needs.body: Hair, colour, bleach residue and conditioner combine into a stubborn plug in traps and in the long, shallow waste runs that often connect a row of backwashes. Where basins sit in the middle of the floor, the waste may run under the floor or in boxing with barely any fall, or go to a small pump. We clear blockages, fit hair catchers and accessible traps, reroute runs with a proper fall and add rodding points so the next clearance is quicker.

needs.title: Hot water for back-to-back washes
needs.body: A salon uses hot water all day in short bursts, often with several basins running at once. An undersized combi or cylinder shows it first as lukewarm rinses at the busiest time. The choice is usually between instantaneous water heaters, electric or gas, which heat on demand but have a limited flow rate, and a cylinder that stores hot water for busy spells. We look at how many basins you run, your gas and electrical supply and the space available before suggesting either.

needs.title: A comfortable, safe place to work
needs.body: Clients sit still with wet hair, so a cold salon gets noticed. Radiators, heating controls and the boiler need to be reliable through winter, while in summer dryers and styling tools add heat that air conditioning can take away. Staff need a working WC and hand-wash basin, and dryers and tongs on overloaded sockets trip circuits. Because we also do electrics and air conditioning, a new water heater with its own circuit, or a cooling unit for the styling floor, is one team's job.

guidance.title: Keep hair out of the waste
guidance.body: Most backwash blockages build slowly, so the early signs are worth acting on: water pooling in the bowl, gurgling, or a smell from the plughole. Fit a hair catcher in every basin and empty it between clients rather than at the end of the day. Avoid tipping leftover colour, bleach or perm solution down the backwash, as residue sticks to hair and hardens in the trap. If several basins slow down at once, the problem is usually further along the shared waste. Clearing it before a busy weekend is far less disruptive than losing a basin on a Saturday.

guidance.title: Planning a refit or new layout
guidance.body: Moving backwashes is where refits most often run into trouble. Before you settle a layout, find out where the nearest soil stack or waste connection is and whether the floor can be lifted or the pipe boxed in. Island backwashes in the middle of the room may need a pump, which works but adds a little noise and upkeep. Leave access panels behind each unit so valves and traps can be reached. If you rent, get your landlord's consent for changes to drainage and the water supply. We can visit before your shopfitter finalises drawings, which saves moving a basin twice.

guidance.title: Choosing how to heat the water
guidance.body: Instantaneous heaters suit smaller salons and barbers with one or two basins: they don't run out, but each has a maximum flow, and a large electric model needs a suitable supply and its own circuit. For three or more basins used together, stored hot water usually copes better. An unvented cylinder gives mains-pressure hot water and must be installed by someone qualified to work on unvented systems; most manufacturers also expect an annual service. London water is hard, so limescale gradually cuts a heater's output. A softener or scale inhibitor is worth considering.

guidance.title: Before your licence inspection
guidance.body: Each London borough sets its own conditions for special treatment licences, so read your council's conditions carefully and ask the licensing team if anything is unclear. Common points include a dedicated hand-wash basin in each treatment area, hot and cold or suitably mixed water, soap and paper towels, and surfaces that are easy to clean. Book any plumbing well before the inspection date, not the week before. If a room is being altered, keep photos and invoices for the work, in case the officer asks what was done and when.

guidance.title: Keep basins for hands only
guidance.body: A hand-wash basin that doubles as a sink for rinsing bowls, brushes or tools is a hygiene risk and an easy point for an inspector to pick up. If you don't have a separate cleaning sink, adding one is usually worthwhile. Keep hand-wash basins clear of stored products, and check that the water warms up within a few seconds of turning the tap. Where very hot water reaches a basin, a thermostatic mixing valve can blend it down to a safer temperature, and we can fit or replace one as part of the job.

guidance.title: Looking after drains and water heaters
guidance.body: Wax, oils, scrubs and skin debris build up in traps faster than most owners expect. Use strainers in pedicure basins, and wipe excess wax and oil into the bin rather than rinsing it away. Run hot and cold water through little-used basins each week: water sitting in pipes is part of the legionella risk that businesses must manage under HSE guidance. Hard London water also scales up small water heaters, so a heater that is slow to warm or keeps tripping may need descaling or replacing.

If you rarely use a second bath or an outside hose, run it for a few minutes each week, because stagnant water can let bacteria grow. We can remove unused pipe runs and fit or replace mixing valves.

intro: Property maintenance for landlords comes down to two jobs: keeping on the right side of the safety rules, and fixing what tenants report before a small fault turns into a big claim. Ninja Plumbers looks after rented flats, houses and HMOs across London and into Surrey for private landlords and letting agents. Our Gas Safe registered engineers carry out annual gas safety checks on domestic boilers and appliances, our registered electricians carry out EICRs, and the same team deals with leaks, blocked drains, boiler breakdowns and void-period refits. We arrange access with you or the tenant, agree the price before work starts and send a clear write-up for your records.

needs.title: A gas safety record every year
needs.body: If a rented home has a gas boiler, hob or fire, you need a gas safety check every year by a Gas Safe registered engineer, and your tenants need a copy of the record. Across a portfolio, a missed renewal date is one of the easiest slips to make. We check each appliance, flue and the ventilation, record what we find and tell you plainly about anything that needs putting right, with a price for the repair.

needs.title: Electrical safety checks every five years
needs.body: Most private tenancies in England need an Electrical Installation Condition Report at least every five years, and sooner if the last report says so. Our registered electricians test the consumer unit, circuits, sockets and fittings, then explain the codes in plain terms. Where the report asks for remedial work, we can do it and give you written confirmation, which you need to keep with the report. Because we do plumbing and electrics, one visit often covers both.

needs.title: Tenant call-outs that get closed off
needs.body: Tenants ring about no hot water, a toilet that will not flush, a dripping ceiling or a boiler showing a fault code. What you need is someone who contacts the tenant, books a time that suits them, fixes the fault and then tells you what was done. We report back to you or your agent with notes, and if the repair goes beyond what you have approved, we call you before carrying on.

needs.title: Void periods and HMO wear
needs.body: The weeks between tenancies are the cheapest time to replace a tired bathroom, swap a failing boiler, upgrade an old fuse box or sort the drip everyone has ignored. HMOs add their own load: several showers running each morning, shared kitchens, more toilets and more blockages. We plan void work to fit your re-letting date, and handle jobs that need more than one trade, such as a new shower with an extractor fan, with one team.

guidance.title: Keep your certificate dates in one place
guidance.body: Put every property's gas safety due date and EICR due date on one list and check it monthly. Current rules let you have the annual gas check done up to two months before the deadline and keep the original anniversary, so there is no penalty for booking early. For electrics, give tenants a copy of the EICR and keep proof of any remedial work. If you use an agent, agree in writing who books these checks, because gaps often appear when each side assumes the other is handling it.

guidance.title: Legionella: your duty and the plumbing side
guidance.body: Landlords have a duty to assess and control the risk from legionella in their properties, as set out in HSE guidance and its Approved Code of Practice, L8. Most ordinary lets are low risk, but empty periods, stored water and unused pipework raise it. Before new tenants move in, run every tap and shower for a few minutes. We do not carry out risk assessments, but we do the plumbing work they point to: removing dead legs, sorting little-used outlets, cylinder and tank work, and fitting thermostatic mixing valves.

guidance.title: Make access and reporting straightforward
guidance.body: Most missed appointments come down to access. Give us the tenant's contact details, any key or concierge arrangement and a spending limit for small repairs. If we cannot get in, we tell you so the visit can be followed up under the tenancy. After each job you get a short note of the fault, the fix and anything to watch, which helps if a dispute about the deposit or repairs comes up later.

needs.title: Many en-suites on one system
needs.body: In a converted townhouse, rooms on the top floor often get the weakest pressure and the longest wait for hot water, while a leak in one en-suite can stain the ceiling of the room below. You need a system where each bathroom can be isolated on its own, so one room can be taken out of use without draining the whole house. We fit isolation valves, balance supplies between floors and trace the leaks that turn up under shower trays.

needs.title: Hot water for the breakfast rush
needs.body: Between seven and nine, most guests shower within the same hour, and that is when a guest house finds out whether its hot water is big enough. A cylinder that recovers too slowly, or a combi boiler asked to serve several rooms, leaves the last guests with a lukewarm shower. We look at stored volume, recovery time and how many outlets run together, then advise on a larger cylinder, an unvented system or better controls.

needs.title: Pumps, stacks and waste
needs.body: Shower pumps work harder in a guest house than anywhere else and tend to fail noisily or without warning. Hair builds up in shower traps, and wipes or sanitary products flushed by guests block soil stacks, usually showing first as a gurgling basin on a lower floor. Where an en-suite has been added far from the stack, a macerator may be doing the work. We repair and replace pumps, clear stacks and fit macerators properly.

needs.title: Gas: domestic boilers and larger plant
needs.body: Many guest houses run on one or two domestic-sized boilers, which our Gas Safe registered engineers service, repair, replace and include in your annual gas safety check. Some small hotels have larger commercial boilers or commercial catering gas equipment such as ranges, fryers or combi ovens in the breakfast kitchen. A brown mark on a ceiling below an en-suite usually means a failed tray seal or waste joint. A shower pump that runs when no tap is open often means a leak somewhere. Report these early.

needs.title: Customer toilets that stand up to a busy night
needs.body: Pub toilets take heavy, rough use in short bursts. Flush valves stick, cisterns get damaged, taps are left running and urinal traps block with debris. Customers notice tired, smelly toilets quickly, and one broken WC soon causes queues. Robust fittings help: vandal-resistant taps, concealed cisterns behind lockable panels, and urinals with a flush controller so the cistern does not keep cycling through the night when the pub is closed.

needs.title: Glasswashers and bar sinks
needs.body: Glasswashers run almost constantly during service and suffer in London's hard water, which leaves glasses cloudy and scales up heaters and spray arms. A softener or dedicated filter on the feed, a proper isolating valve and a waste that can take a fast discharge all help. Bar sinks, ice machine feeds and drip tray wastes also need to drain freely. Where we can, we fix leaks behind the bar without taking the counter apart.

needs.title: Cellars that stay dry
needs.body: Cellars collect water from cleaning, spills, condensation and sometimes groundwater. Many rely on a floor gully or a sump pump to lift water up to the drain, so a failed pump or blocked gully can flood the cellar within a shift. Non-return valves stop the drain backing up, and a high-level alarm warns you before water reaches stock or electrics. We keep to drainage and pumps; beer lines and cellar cooling are for your dispense technician.

needs.title: Kitchens and heating
needs.body: If you serve food, the kitchen needs the same care as any restaurant: a grease trap, hand-wash basins with hot and cold running water, and sound dishwasher connections. Old pubs often have awkward heating, with long pipe runs and radiators fighting draughty doors. Our Gas Safe engineers work on domestic-sized boilers. Larger commercial boilers and catering gas equipment need engineers with commercial gas qualifications, and we will tell you straight if yours is beyond what we do.

If the drain backs up in heavy rain, a non-return valve may be missing or stuck. Consider a second pump or an alarm if the cellar has flooded before. needs.title: Showers that stay hot and steady
needs.body: A row of changing room showers used at once, straight after a class, puts heavy demand on both hot water and pressure. needs.title: Drains that cope with hair, soap and heavy use
needs.body: Hair, soap residue, body wash and grit build up quickly in shower traps and floor gullies, especially in shared wet areas. A slow drain means standing water, slippery floors and complaints at the front desk. Linear drains and wet room formers need to be laid to the right fall, or water spreads across the changing room. Regular trap cleaning helps, and when a drain keeps blocking, a camera survey can show whether the pipe itself is the problem.

needs.title: Safe water in showers used unevenly
needs.body: Some showers are used all day while others, often in a quieter changing room or an accessible cubicle, sit idle. Showers create a fine spray, so stagnant water in little-used outlets and dead legs is a legionella concern. The gym operator, or the landlord, has a duty to manage that risk under HSE guidance (ACoP L8). We handle the plumbing side: removing dead legs, reworking pipework and fitting or replacing thermostatic mixing valves.

needs.title: Cool, well-ventilated training spaces

guidance.title: Sizing hot water for your busiest hour
guidance.body: Work out how many showers could run at once after your biggest class, then think about how long each person typically showers. That peak, rather than the daily total, decides how much hot water you need stored and how quickly it must recover. Keep stored water hot enough to control bacteria and use thermostatic mixing valves to bring it down to a safe showering temperature at the outlet. If your cylinder is struggling, a larger unit or a second one may be the answer.

guidance.title: Weekly checks for your team
guidance.body: Give staff a short weekly checklist. Run any shower that has not been used that week for a few minutes, pull hair out of shower and basin traps, and look for water pooling away from the drain. Report any shower that runs too hot, too cold or keeps dripping after it shuts off. Check under vanity units for leaks, and make sure the changing room extractor fans are actually running. Small faults found early are simpler to fix.

guidance.title: Scald protection at the tap
guidance.body: The Early Years Foundation Stage framework expects settings to provide suitable toilets and hand-washing facilities, and you are responsible for keeping children safe around hot water. The usual protection at basins is a thermostatic mixing valve set to a lower outlet temperature. Guidance commonly points to around 43°C for basins used by young children, but follow your own risk assessment. Get into the habit of feeling the water at each basin children use, and report it if it seems hotter than usual. We can fit a new valve or replace one that has failed.

guidance.title: Common failures to watch for
guidance.body: Most nursery callouts come from a handful of problems. Toys, wipes and too much paper block toilets, so keep wipes in a lidded bin and help children use a little paper at a time. Cisterns in small WCs take rough handling, and a flush that keeps running wastes water and can hide a slow leak. Sticky taps and loose basins are worth reporting before they get worse. Walk round the toilets once a week and note anything that drips, rocks or keeps running, so small repairs can be done together in one visit.

guidance.title: Holidays, closures and legionella
guidance.body: Water that sits in pipes over a holiday or long weekend is a legionella risk. The setting, or its landlord, has a duty to manage that risk under HSE guidance, which includes dealing with little-used outlets. Before children come back, run each tap and shower for a few minutes, cold then hot. Unused basins and pipework left from old layouts are best removed rather than flushed forever, and we can cut out those dead legs. Holiday closures are also the best time for bigger jobs, such as a new toilet area or boiler replacement.

guidance.title: Getting the heating on in time
guidance.body: Thick stone and brick walls soak up heat, so a church, temple or hall used on a weekend morning may need the heating on for several hours beforehand, sometimes from the evening before. A programmable timer, or an optimising controller that learns how long the building takes to warm, saves guesswork and wasted gas. Keep internal doors closed and deal with obvious draughts. A low background setting between services can help protect the fabric, organ and furnishings from damp, but check with your architect or your faith body's building advisers on what suits your building.

guidance.title: Planning an ablution or wudu area
guidance.body: Start with numbers: how many people wash at the busiest prayer, and roughly how long each takes. That peak decides how many wudu positions you need, how much hot water must be stored or heated, and how large the drains and gullies should be. Fix seats at a comfortable height with taps within easy reach, and add a grab rail for older worshippers. Floors need a slip-resistant finish laid to fall, with walls that wipe clean. Plan an accessible position, separate areas where your community needs them, and an extractor fan to keep damp down.

The trustees, committee or other body responsible for the building has a duty to manage that risk under HSE guidance (ACoP L8), and running taps for a few minutes before a group arrives is a sensible habit. guidance.title: Emptying the trap and knowing when it is full
guidance.body: A sediment trap only works if someone empties it. Busy teaching studios may need to do it weekly, quieter ones less often, so make it part of the closing routine. Signs it is full: the sink drains slowly, water sits in the basin, clay appears in the outlet, or there is a stale or eggy smell from standing water. Scoop or lift out the settled clay, let it dry and bin it or reclaim it, never tip it down a toilet or outside gully. Check the seals and lid when you put it back so it does not leak.

guidance.body: It is an offence to put anything into a public sewer that is likely to damage it or block it, and Thames Water can take action over blockages caused by materials that should not be in the drains. Inks and paints are different: follow the disposal instructions on each product, and never pour solvents, white spirit or oil paint down any sink. faqs.q: What is the best way to heat a yoga studio?
faqs.a: For most studios, underfloor heating is the most comfortable option, because warmth comes up evenly through the floor where students practise. The easiest moment to lay it is while the studio is being refurbished and the old floor is lifted. If you keep radiators, place them clear of mat areas and set a schedule that starts well ahead, so the first students step into warmth.

faqs.q: Can you install infrared heaters for hot yoga?
faqs.a: Yes. Our registered electricians fit infrared panels and convector heaters on dedicated circuits, check whether your fuse board can take the extra load, and test everything before classes begin. We normally plan the heaters alongside extraction or air conditioning, so the room can heat up for class and then be cleared of warmth and moisture afterwards.

faqs.q: How do I stop condensation and mould in my hot yoga room?
faqs.a: Start with extraction that suits the size of the room and the number of students, running during and after every heated class. Air conditioning helps dry and cool the space between sessions. Keep an eye on corners, window reveals and ceilings. If mould keeps coming back, we can look at the fan size, ducting and where the moist air actually ends up.

faqs.q: Can I add a shower to my yoga studio?
faqs.a: Often, yes, even in a studio above a shop or in a converted building. We check the water pressure at your floor, how hot water will be supplied and where the waste can run. If a gravity drain is not practical, a pumped waste may work. You get a clear explanation and an agreed price before anything begins.

faqs.q: Can you do the work without disrupting classes?
faqs.a: Yes. We book noisy jobs before you open, after the last session or on a closed day, and keep any daytime work well away from the practice room. Everyone who comes is a DBS-checked member of our own staff, and they tidy as they go. For a leak or a blocked WC that cannot wait, there is a 24/7 emergency callout.

guidance.title: Plan hot water around your busiest slots
guidance.body: Look at your fullest early and lunchtime classes, count how many clients shower afterwards and note how soon the following session finishes. That peak decides the size of your hot water system far more than the daily total. Instantaneous electric heaters can struggle with several showers running together, while a stored system needs enough capacity and quick recovery. Store water hot, then rely on thermostatic mixing valves to temper it at each shower head. Having those valves tested and serviced keeps temperatures consistent for every client.

guidance.title: Refitting without cancelling classes
guidance.body: A changing room refit rarely needs the studio to close. Split the work into stages, keeping one set of showers open while the other is rebuilt, and schedule loud tasks such as breaking out screed for evenings and weekends. Agree a programme before bookings open for the affected weeks, so the timetable can flex if needed. Choose valves with accessible isolation and sealed, wipe-clean surfaces. Because we cover plumbing, electrics and air conditioning, the trades are coordinated rather than waiting on each other.

guidance.title: Quiet showers and the towel laundry
guidance.body: Studios that add a rehab or clinical pilates room with its own shower sometimes find it barely used. Legionella control is a legal duty for the operator or landlord, set out in HSE's ACoP L8, and water standing in quiet outlets falls within it. Run such showers weekly and record it. For towels, a washing machine with its own isolation valves and a correctly sized standpipe waste avoids floods and drain smells. Clean the machine's filter and check the hoses every few months.

faqs.q: How much hot water does a reformer pilates studio need?
faqs.a: It depends on how many clients shower after each class and how tightly your sessions run, not on the daily total. We count showers, look at your timetable and check the incoming supply, then recommend a cylinder size or other system that recovers between classes. The options are explained and a price is agreed before work starts.

faqs.q: Do I need air conditioning in my reformer studio?
faqs.a: In most converted units, yes. Reformer rooms fill with people working hard, and shopfronts and roof lights add heat. Our F-Gas certified engineers survey the room, class size and where an outdoor unit could sit, then recommend a system. If you lease the unit, check the lease and speak to the landlord before external units go on the building.

faqs.q: Can you fit out a pilates studio in an empty retail unit?
faqs.a: Yes. We plan and install the plumbing, hot water, changing rooms, WCs and electrics, and our F-Gas engineers fit the air conditioning. We begin by checking the water supply, drainage routes and power available, since shell units are often very basic. Having one team for these trades keeps the programme simpler and avoids gaps between contractors.

faqs.q: Can you add hairdryer sockets and lighting to our vanity area?
faqs.a: Yes. Our registered electricians add sockets at a practical height near mirrors, install good task lighting and check that the circuits and fuse board can take several hairdryers running together. Everything is tested and certified. We can do this alongside basin or shower work, so the vanity area is finished in one go.

faqs.q: Will a changing room refit mean closing the studio?
